To use `#[tokio::main]` with the multi-threaded runtime, you need the `macros` and `rt-multi-thread` features ([tokio crate documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/)). The `macros` feature enables the `#[tokio::main]` attribute macro itself, while `rt-multi-thread` enables the multi-threaded work-stealing scheduler.

## Required features

- `macros`: Enables the `#[tokio::main]` and `#[tokio::test]` attribute macros ([tokio crate documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/))
- `rt-multi-thread`: Enables the multi-threaded scheduler ([tokio crate documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/))

## What the multi-threaded runtime does

- The multi-threaded runtime is the default flavor and executes futures on a thread pool using a work-stealing strategy ([tokio #[tokio::main] documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/attr.main.html))
- It spawns worker threads by default matching the number of CPU cores on the system, though this can be configured with the `worker_threads` option ([tokio #[tokio::main] documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/attr.main.html))

## Example Cargo.toml

- In your `Cargo.toml`: `tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }`

Enabling `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` in serde requires adding the `derive` feature to your `serde` dependency. To use it, add `serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }` to your Cargo.toml, then import and apply the derive macros to your structs and enums ([Using derive · Serde](https://serde.rs/derive.html)).

## Enabling the derive macros

- Add `serde` with the `derive` feature to Cargo.toml: `serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }` ([Using derive · Serde](https://serde.rs/derive.html)).
- Import the macros in your module with `use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};` and apply them to your types with `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` ([Using derive · Serde](https://serde.rs/derive.html)).
- The derive feature is behind a feature flag because the macro implementation adds compile time ([Feature flags · Serde](https://serde.rs/feature-flags.html)).

## The Serialize and Deserialize trait methods

- The `Serialize` trait has a single required method `serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>` where `S: Serializer`, which maps your type into the Serde data model by invoking methods on the given Serializer ([Implementing Serialize · Serde](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html)).
- The `Deserialize` trait has a single required method `deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>` where `D: Deserializer<'de>`, which reconstructs your type from the Serde data model ([serde - Rust - Docs.rs](https://docs.rs/serde/latest/serde/trait.Deserialize.html)).
- The `'de` lifetime on `Deserialize` represents the lifetime of data that may be borrowed by the type during deserialization ([serde - Rust - Docs.rs](https://docs.rs/serde/latest/serde/trait.Deserialize.html)).

Sources:

2. [Implementing Serialize · Serde](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html)
3. [serde - Rust - Docs.rs](https://docs.rs/serde/latest/serde/trait.Deserialize.html)

The clap derive API lets you define command-line arguments by deriving `Parser` on a struct, where each field becomes an argument. The `derive` feature flag must be enabled in `Cargo.toml`.

## Setting up the derive API

- Enable the `derive` feature with `cargo add clap --features derive` or by adding `clap = { version = "...", features = ["derive"] }` to `Cargo.toml` ([Clap Derive Parser Macro](https://rust-lang-nursery.github.io/rust-cookbook/cli/clap-derive.html)).
- Add `#[derive(Parser)]` to your struct and call `.parse()` to parse arguments ([Tutorial for the Derive API](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/_tutorial/)).

## Defining different argument types

- **Positional arguments**: By default, struct fields define positional arguments, like `name: String` ([Tutorial for the Derive API](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/_tutorial/)).
- **Options (named flags)**: Use `#[arg(short, long)]` to add short (`-n`) and long (`--name`) flags to a field ([Tutorial for the Derive API](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/_tutorial/)).
- **Boolean flags**: Fields of type `bool` default to `SetTrue` action, so `--verbose` without a value sets it to true ([Tutorial for the Derive API](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/_tutorial/)).
- **Optional arguments**: Wrap the type in `Option<T>` to make an argument optional instead of required ([Clap Derive Parser Macro](https://rust-lang-nursery.github.io/rust-cookbook/cli/clap-derive.html)).
- **Multiple values**: Use `Vec<T>` to accept multiple values with `Append` action ([Tutorial for the Derive API](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/_tutorial/)).

## Common attributes

- Use `#[command(...)]` attributes on the struct for application-level settings like `version`, `about`, and `long_about` ([Tutorial for the Derive API](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/_tutorial/)).
- Use `#[arg(...)]` attributes on fields for argument-specific settings like `default_value_t`, `value_parser`, and `requires` ([Tutorial for the Derive API](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/_tutorial/)).

Anyhow provides two methods to attach context to errors: `context()` for eager evaluation and `with_context()` for lazy evaluation, and it supports no_std mode by disabling the default "std" feature in Cargo.toml while providing a global allocator.

## Attaching context to errors

- Use `.context(msg)` to wrap an error with a static context message ([anyhow documentation](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/trait.Context.html)). The context is evaluated immediately when the method is called.
- Use `.with_context(|| msg)` to wrap an error with a lazily-evaluated context message ([anyhow documentation](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/trait.Context.html)). The closure is only executed if an error actually occurs, making this more efficient when context computation is expensive.
- Both methods work on `Result<T, E>` and `Option<T>`, and you can downcast to either the context type or the original error type even after adding context ([anyhow documentation](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/trait.Context.html)).

## Using anyhow in no_std

- Disable the default "std" feature in Cargo.toml: `anyhow = { version = "1.0", default-features = false }` ([anyhow documentation](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/)).
- Almost all of the same API is available in no_std mode and works identically to the std version ([anyhow documentation](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/)).
- For Rust versions older than 1.81, you may need to add `.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with non-Anyhow error types in functions returning Anyhow's error type ([anyhow documentation](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/)).

To compile and reuse a regex with Rust's regex crate, use `std::sync::LazyLock` (stable since Rust 1.80) or the `once_cell` crate to create a lazily-initialized static that compiles the regex once and shares it safely across threads. Alternatively, use the `regex!` macro for compile-time compilation. The crate does not support backreferences, lookaround assertions, or atomic groups—deliberate omissions that allow linear-time matching guarantees.

## Compiling and Reusing Regexes

- Use `std::sync::LazyLock` to compile a regex once into a static and reuse it automatically: `static EMAIL: LazyLock<Regex> = LazyLock::new(|| Regex::new(r"...").unwrap());` ([Rust regex crate](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)).
- The `regex!` macro automatically handles lazy compilation and reuse, useful inside functions to avoid the overhead of repeated `Regex::new` calls ([Rust regex crate](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)).
- Regex compilation is expensive (microseconds to milliseconds), so compiling in loops or hot functions is an anti-pattern that prevents internal optimizations ([Rust regex crate](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)).
- A single compiled `Regex` is thread-safe and can be freely shared across threads using `Sync`, with no additional memory cost from cloning ([Rust regex crate](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)).

## Unsupported Features

- The crate does not support backreferences or lookaround assertions, a deliberate design choice to guarantee linear-time matching and prevent catastrophic backtracking ([Rust regex crate](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)).
- If backreferences or lookaround are required, use the `fancy-regex` crate, which layers a backtracking engine on top of the standard regex crate ([Rust Regex Guide](https://janeer.com/guides/rust-regex/)).
- The crate uses finite automata matching (like Go's RE2), which structurally prevents these features to maintain `O(m * n)` worst-case time complexity where `m` is the regex size and `n` is the haystack length ([Rust Regex Guide](https://janeer.com/guides/rust-regex/)).

Sources:
1. [Rust regex crate](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)
2. [Rust Regex Guide](https://janeer.com/guides/rust-regex/)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly explains one-time compilation and reuse, identifies look-around and backreferences as unsupported, and states the O(m * n) bound without contradicting any reference nugget.

The `tracing` crate records spans and events using macros, and you install a subscriber in an executable to collect that trace data. Spans represent periods of time with beginning and end points, while events represent moments in time; both are recorded through macros and then collected by a subscriber that you set globally or locally.

## Recording Spans and Events

- Create spans with the [`span!`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/macro.span.html) macro, which returns a `Span` struct, then call [`Span::enter()`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/struct.Span.html#method.enter) to enter it and get a RAII guard that exits when dropped ([Tracing docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)):
- Use the [`#[instrument]`](https://docs.rs/tracing-attributes/latest/tracing_attributes/attr.instrument.html) attribute macro on functions to automatically create and enter a span with the function's name, recording function arguments as fields ([Tracing docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)):
- Record events with the [`event!`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/macro.event.html) macro or shorthand macros like `info!`, `debug!`, `warn!`, and `error!` ([Tracing docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)):
- Add structured fields to spans and events using the syntax `field_name = field_value`, separated by commas ([Tracing docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)):

## Installing a Subscriber in an Executable

- Use [`tracing_subscriber::fmt::init()`](https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/latest/tracing_subscriber/fmt/fn.init.html) to create and globally install a subscriber configured by the `RUST_LOG` environment variable ([GitHub - tokio-rs/tracing](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing)):
- Alternatively, build a subscriber manually and install it with [`tracing::subscriber::set_global_default()`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/subscriber/fn.set_global_default.html) or use [`tracing::subscriber::with_default()`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/subscriber/fn.with_default.html) to set it locally for a closure ([Tracing docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)):
- Libraries should **not** call `set_global_default()` to avoid conflicts; only executables should install the global subscriber ([Tracing docs](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)):

Sources:

2. [GitHub - tokio-rs/tracing](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing)

`fsPromises.mkdir()` resolves with `undefined` when `recursive` is false, or with the first directory path created when `recursive` is true (or `undefined` if the entire path already existed). - Without `recursive` or with `recursive: false`, the promise always resolves with `undefined` ([fsPromises.mkdir() — Node.js Function Reference](https://soundscode.com/nodejs/fs-promises-mkdir)).
- With `recursive: true`, the promise resolves with the first directory path that was created, or `undefined` if the entire path already existed ([fsPromises.mkdir() — Node.js Function Reference](https://soundscode.com/nodejs/fs-promises-mkdir)).

## The recursive option

- When `recursive: true` is set, `fsPromises.mkdir()` behaves like the Unix `mkdir -p` command, creating all missing parent directories in the path ([fsPromises.mkdir() — Node.js Function Reference](https://soundscode.com/nodejs/fs-promises-mkdir)).
- With `recursive: true`, the method resolves without error even if the directory already exists, instead of throwing `EEXIST` ([fsPromises.mkdir() — Node.js Function Reference](https://soundscode.com/nodejs/fs-promises-mkdir)).
- The `recursive` option is useful to detect whether you created the directory yourself: if the resolved value is `undefined`, the path already existed ([fsPromises.mkdir() — Node.js Function Reference](https://soundscode.com/nodejs/fs-promises-mkdir)).

Error E0502 occurs when you try to mutate data while an immutable reference to it is still active. Rust enforces a strict rule: you can have many immutable references or exactly one mutable reference, but never both at the same time. This prevents data races and undefined behavior.

## What the error means

- [The official Rust documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0502.html) explains that "a variable already borrowed with a certain mutability (either mutable or immutable) was borrowed again with a different mutability." The compiler blocks this because allowing mutation while a reference is reading the data could cause the reference to read garbage, partial updates, or corrupted values.

## How to fix it

- [Separate the borrows into distinct scopes](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/error-e0502-cannot-borrow-as-mutable/): ensure the immutable borrow ends before the mutable borrow begins. Modern Rust uses Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL), which end borrows at the last use of a reference rather than at the end of a scope block. Move the mutation after the last use of the immutable reference.

## Common patterns and solutions

- **Extract values before mutating**: If you need to read a field and then mutate the struct, clone or copy the value first to break the borrow chain.
- **Use the `entry` API for HashMap**: When checking if a key exists and conditionally inserting, use `entry().or_insert()` instead of separate `get()` and `insert()` calls, which avoids holding a reference while mutating.
- **Use `split_at_mut` for slices**: When you need two mutable references to non-overlapping parts of a collection, `split_at_mut()` lets the compiler verify they don't conflict.
- **Use `retain` for filtering collections**: Instead of iterating and mutating a vector, use methods like `retain()` that handle the borrow internally.
- **Interior mutability as a last resort**: `RefCell<T>` allows mutation through an immutable reference but moves the check to runtime; use it only when the borrow checker's compile-time restrictions are too rigid.

Rust error E0382 occurs when a value is used after its ownership has been moved to another variable, violating Rust's ownership system that prevents multiple owners from trying to clean up the same allocation. This error protects against use-after-free bugs by ensuring each non-`Copy` value has only one owner at a time.

## What causes the error

- **Moving a value to a function:** When a function takes a value by ownership (not by reference), ownership transfers and the original binding cannot be used afterward ([Fix Rust E0382: use of moved value](https://learningrust.org/guides/fix-rust-e0382)).
- **Non-Copy types:** Types like `String`, `Vec<T>`, and custom structs without the `Copy` trait trigger this error. Primitive types like `i32` implement `Copy` and avoid E0382 because they are implicitly duplicated ([Error code E0382](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0382.html)).

## Ways to fix it

- **Use references (preferred):** Pass a reference `&value` instead of moving the value, letting the function borrow without taking ownership ([Fix Rust E0382: use of moved value](https://learningrust.org/guides/fix-rust-e0382)).
- **Clone the value:** Call `.clone()` to create a duplicate owned allocation, allowing both the original and the function to have separate copies ([Error code E0382](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0382.html)).
- **Implement Copy:** For simple types you control, derive or implement `Copy` to enable implicit cloning with no runtime cost ([Error code E0382](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0382.html)).
- **Use Rc and RefCell for shared ownership:** When you need multiple owners and mutable shared access, wrap the value in `Rc<RefCell<T>>` for reference counting and runtime borrow checking ([Error code E0382](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0382.html)).

1. [Fix Rust E0382: use of moved value](https://learningrust.org/guides/fix-rust-e0382)

PostgreSQL error SQLSTATE 23505 is a "unique constraint violation" that occurs when you try to insert or update a row with a value that already exists in a column (or combination of columns) protected by a unique constraint or primary key. The error message names the specific constraint and conflicting value to help you diagnose the issue.

## What the Error Means

- [PostgreSQL Error 23505](https://www.sqliz.com/posts/fix-error-23505-postgresql-unique-violation/) means "an INSERT or UPDATE would duplicate a value protected by a primary key, unique constraint, or unique index". The error details show which constraint was violated and what value caused the conflict.

## Common Causes

- **Explicit duplicates**: Trying to insert a row with a value that already exists in a unique column like email or username.
- **Out-of-sync sequences**: After bulk imports or manual data inserts, the auto-increment sequence can fall behind the actual maximum ID in the table, causing new inserts to collide with existing IDs.
- **Race conditions**: Multiple concurrent transactions attempting to insert the same unique value simultaneously.

## How to Avoid the Error on Insert

- **Use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING**: Skip the insert silently if a duplicate exists: `INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('john@example.com') ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;`.
- **Use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE** (upsert): Update the existing row instead of inserting: `INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('john@example.com', 'John') ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name;`.
- **Reset out-of-sync sequences**: After data imports with explicit IDs, resync the sequence: `SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('users', 'id'), (SELECT MAX(id) FROM users));`.
- **Handle errors in application code**: Catch the unique violation exception and respond gracefully rather than letting it propagate to users.

Sources:
1. [PostgreSQL Error 23505](https://www.sqliz.com/posts/fix-error-23505-postgresql-unique-violation/)

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time; the server is rate-limiting you and asking you to slow down. Your client should not retry immediately, but instead honor the `Retry-After` header if present, implement exponential backoff with jitter, and reduce its steady request rate to avoid hitting the limit again.

## Understanding the response

- 429 means the server rejected your request without processing it, so the request is safe to retry even for non-idempotent methods like POST ([429 Too Many Requests](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429)).
- Rate limits can be per API key, per IP address, per account, per endpoint, or per token count; multiple limits can apply simultaneously ([Handling HTTP 429 Too Many Requests: Rate Limiting Headers, Exponential Backoff & Jitter](https://wtool.dev/guides/http-429-rate-limiting-retry-after-backoff)).

## How to respond

- **Honor Retry-After:** If the response includes a `Retry-After` header (either a number of seconds or an HTTP date), wait at least that long before retrying ([429 Too Many Requests: Fix It with Retry-After and Backoff](https://howhttpworks.com/debug/429-too-many-requests-fix)).
- **Use exponential backoff with full jitter:** When there's no `Retry-After`, apply exponential backoff where the delay for attempt `n` is a random value between 0 and `min(cap, base * 2^n)`. This breaks synchronization between clients and prevents "thundering herd" retries that crash the server ([429 Too Many Requests: Fix It with Retry-After and Backoff](https://howhttpworks.com/debug/429-too-many-requests-fix)).
- **Cap retry attempts and surface failures:** Set a maximum number of retries (typically 4-5) and a total wait time cap, then fail rather than loop forever ([429 Too Many Requests: Fix It with Retry-After and Backoff](https://howhttpworks.com/debug/429-too-many-requests-fix)).
- **Reduce your request rate:** Implement client-side pacing by limiting concurrency, batching calls, caching responses, and spreading scheduled jobs to stay below the limit in the first place ([429 Too Many Requests: Fix It with Retry-After and Backoff](https://howhttpworks.com/debug/429-too-many-requests-fix)).

[What's New in Go 1.27: A Complete Guide](https://levelupgo.dev/blog/whats-new-in-go-1-27)

## Language changes

- Generic methods now allow a method declaration to declare its own type parameters, independent of the receiver type, enabling method chaining and better API design for concrete types. However, interface methods still cannot declare type parameters, and generic methods cannot implement interface methods. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- Struct literals now accept any valid field selector as a key, not just top-level field names, which simplifies embedded field initialization. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- Function type inference is generalized to apply whenever a generic function is assigned to or converted to a matching function type, not only at call sites. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)

## Standard library and security

- `encoding/json` is now backed by the v2 implementation with preserved v1 behavior by default, while `encoding/json/v2` offers stricter defaults (rejects invalid UTF-8, duplicate object keys), and `encoding/json/jsontext` provides lower-level token and value processing. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- A new `uuid` package in the standard library eliminates the need for third-party dependencies, with `UUID` defined as `[16]byte` making values comparable and usable as map keys, and generators including `New`, `NewV4`, and `NewV7` for time-sortable keys. [What's New in Go 1.27: A Developer's Practical Guide](https://www.adilaidev.com/blog/whats-new-in-go-127-a-developers-practical-guide/)
- `crypto/mldsa` implements the post-quantum ML-DSA signature scheme from FIPS 204 with three parameter sets (44, 65, 87), supported in `crypto/x509` and `crypto/tls`, plus `MLKEM1024` key exchange for quantum-safe TLS 1.3 handshakes. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)

## Tooling and performance

- `go test` now runs the `stdversion` vet check by default to catch use of standard library symbols newer than the module's Go version directive allows. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- `go fix` adds new modernizers (`atomictypes`, `embedlit`, `slicesbackward`, `unsafefuncs`) to rewrite older patterns to current idioms, and `go mod tidy` now automatically consolidates duplicate require blocks for modules on Go 1.27 or later. [What's New in Go 1.27: A Developer's Practical Guide](https://www.adilaidev.com/blog/whats-new-in-go-127-a-developers-practical-guide/)
- Memory allocations under 80 bytes are up to 30% faster through size-specialized allocation routines, with approximately 1% overall improvement in allocation-heavy programs at the cost of 60 KB additional binary size. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)
- Goroutine leak profiling is now generally available (graduated from experimental), and tracebacks now include `runtime/pprof` goroutine labels for modules with Go 1.27 or later directives, improving debuggability. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)

Sources:
1. [What's New in Go 1.27: A Complete Guide](https://levelupgo.dev/blog/whats-new-in-go-1-27)
2. [Go 1.27 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.27)

Python 3.15's headline features include lazy imports for faster startup, new built-in types (`frozendict` and `sentinel`), UTF-8 as the default encoding, unpacking in comprehensions, and a stable ABI for free-threaded builds. The final 3.15.0 release is scheduled for [Friday, October 9, 2026](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3150rc3/).

## Language and interpreter improvements

- [Lazy imports](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html) via the `lazy` keyword reduce startup time by deferring module loading until first use.
- [`frozendict`](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html) is a new immutable mapping type added as a builtin.
- [`sentinel`](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html) is a new builtin type for creating unique sentinel values with concise representation.
- [UTF-8 is now the default encoding](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html) across the interpreter.
- [Unpacking in comprehensions](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html) allows `*` and `**` operators in list, set, and dict comprehensions.

## Performance and profiling

- The [experimental JIT compiler](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3150rc3/) has been significantly upgraded, with 7-8% geometric mean performance improvement on x86-64 Linux and 11-12% speedup on AArch64 macOS.
- [Tachyon](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html), a new high-frequency statistical sampling profiler, enables low-overhead performance analysis at rates up to 1,000,000 Hz.
- [Frame pointers are enabled by default](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html) for improved system-level observability.

## C API and typing

- [Stable ABI for free-threaded builds](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3150rc3/) is now available.
- New typing features including [TypedDict with typed extra items](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html), [`TypeForm`](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html), and [disjoint bases in the type system](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html).

PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4, released September 24, 2026, is a stabilization release focused on hardening new features rather than adding major functionality, with significant feature reverts to prioritize reliability and predictable release schedules ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)).

## Key Features in PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4

- **REPACK CONCURRENTLY:** A built-in replacement for VACUUM FULL that reclaims dead tuples and reorganizes the heap while allowing reads and writes to continue uninterrupted, eliminating the need for the third-party `pg_repack` extension ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4: What Survived 53 Feature Reverts](https://byteiota.com/postgresql-19-beta-4-whats-actually-in-it/)).
- **Parallel Autovacuum with Priority Scoring:** A new `pg_stat_autovacuum_scores` view provides visibility into why tables are queued for autovacuum, with parallel index processing and tunable `autovacuum_max_parallel_workers` and per-table `autovacuum_parallel_workers` settings ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4: What Survived 53 Feature Reverts](https://byteiota.com/postgresql-19-beta-4-whats-actually-in-it/)).
- **Async I/O Auto-Scaling:** The `io_method=worker` feature now auto-scales background worker count based on actual I/O demand with new GUCs (`io_min_workers`, `io_max_workers`, `io_worker_idle_timeout`), and EXPLAIN ANALYZE now includes per-node AIO statistics ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4: What Survived 53 Feature Reverts](https://byteiota.com/postgresql-19-beta-4-whats-actually-in-it/)).
- **ON CONFLICT Upsert Improvements:** The new ON CONFLICT syntax lets developers see which row caused the conflict and return its current data in a single query ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4: What Survived 53 Feature Reverts](https://byteiota.com/postgresql-19-beta-4-whats-actually-in-it/)).
- **Monitoring Enhancements:** New `pg_stat_lock` view surfaces per-lock-type contention statistics, and per-process `log_min_messages` configuration allows granular logging control ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4: What Survived 53 Feature Reverts](https://byteiota.com/postgresql-19-beta-4-whats-actually-in-it/)).

## Reverted Features

- **SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ):** Support for property graph queries was reverted due to unresolved design concerns ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)).
- **Partition Operations:** Both `ALTER TABLE ... MERGE PARTITIONS` and `ALTER TABLE ... SPLIT PARTITIONS` were reverted due to design issues discovered during beta review ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)).
- **Temporal Updates/Deletes:** Support for the `FOR PORTION OF` clause for temporal updates and deletes was reverted ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)).
- **Online Data Checksum Control:** Online enabling and disabling of data checksums was reverted ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)).
- **LC_COLLATE Postmaster Change:** A change that forced `LC_COLLATE` to `C` in the postmaster process was reverted ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)).
- **Removed Functions:** The functions `pg_get_role_ddl()`, `pg_get_tablespace_ddl()`, and `pg_get_database_ddl()` were removed ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)).

## Context on Reverts

- Across four beta rounds, the development team reverted 53 features total, reflecting the PostgreSQL community's commitment to reliability and predictable release schedules ([PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4: What Survived 53 Feature Reverts](https://byteiota.com/postgresql-19-beta-4-whats-actually-in-it/)).

Sources:
1. [PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-19-beta-4-released-3386/)
2. [PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4: What Survived 53 Feature Reverts](https://byteiota.com/postgresql-19-beta-4-whats-actually-in-it/)

Kubernetes v1.37 (Garhwal), released August 26, 2026, includes 67 enhancements with 16 graduating to Stable, 23 to Beta, and 27 entering Alpha, focused on improving AI/ML workload scheduling, storage efficiency, and control plane resilience [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).

## Stable Graduations

- **Resilient watchcache initialization** prevents traffic spikes against etcd during API server startup and recovery by safely rejecting excess requests with HTTP 429 responses rather than overwhelming the cache [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale to zero** enables workloads using object or external metrics to scale down to zero Pods when idle, reducing costs for queue consumers and batch jobs [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **metrics.k8s.io API** graduates to Stable after nearly nine years in Beta, providing a standard way to retrieve CPU and memory usage for pods and nodes [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **Pod certificates and ClusterTrustBundles** provide first-class support for distributing private keys, X.509 certificates, and trust bundles to Pods via projected volumes [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **DRA features** including ResourceClaim status with network interface data, extended resource request handling, device taints and tolerations, and standard NUMA node attributes all reach Stable [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).

## Beta Features

- **Gang scheduling** graduates to Beta with workload-aware preemption, ensuring that defined Pod groups are scheduled only when the cluster has sufficient resources for the entire group [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **Native histogram support for Kubernetes metrics** uses dynamic exponential bucket boundaries instead of fixed ones, improving storage efficiency and query performance [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **etcd RangeStream support** adds server-streaming RPC to paginate responses with adaptive chunk sizing, significantly reducing memory usage during watch cache initialization [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **Memory QoS** graduates to Beta, using cgroups v2 controls to protect requested memory from reclamation and throttle usage before reaching hard limits [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).

## Notable Deprecations

- **kube-dns is deprecated**, with CoreDNS as the standard since v1.13; no new packages expected after v1.40 [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).
- **kube-proxy's ipvs mode is deprecated**, expected to be disabled by default in v1.40 and removed entirely by v1.43 [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/).

Sources:
1. [Kubernetes v1.37: Garhwal](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/08/26/kubernetes-v1-37-release/)

Cross-compiling a Rust binary for aarch64 Linux with cargo requires adding the target and then building with the `--target` flag. For pure Rust projects, `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` followed by `cargo build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` is often sufficient ([Cross-compilation - The rustup book](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/cross-compilation.html)) (quote: "To compile to other platforms you must install other target platforms. This is done with the rustup target add command").

## Basic setup

- Add the aarch64 target with `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([The rustup book](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/cross-compilation.html)).
- Build using `cargo build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, which places binaries in `target/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/` ([Cross-Compiling - Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html)).
- Optionally set a default target in `.cargo/config.toml` to avoid repeating the flag ([Cross-Compiling - Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html)).

## When complications arise

- If your crate has native C dependencies (like OpenSSL), you need those libraries compiled for the target. On Debian-based systems, install the cross-compiler and target libraries: `sudo apt install gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu libssl-dev:arm64`, then set `CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` ([Cross-Compiling - Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html)).
- The `cross` tool automates this by running compilation in Docker containers with preinstalled toolchains, eliminating the need to install cross-compilation dependencies on your host: `cargo install cross` followed by `cross build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([Cross-Compiling - Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html)).
- `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` is Tier 1 supported, so binaries built for it are widely compatible; the target can be cross-compiled from any host ([aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu - The rustc book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/rustc/platform-support/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.html)).

Sources:
1. [Cross-compilation - The rustup book](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/cross-compilation.html) (unsupported: the cited page does not contain the quoted text)
2. [Cross-Compiling - Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html)
3. [aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu - The rustc book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/rustc/platform-support/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.html)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly gives the target, rustup and Cargo commands, and linker environment variable, but its claim that those commands are often sufficient for pure Rust projects conflicts with the stated typical need for a target linker.

To squash the last 3 commits in git, use `git rebase -i HEAD~3` to start an interactive rebase, then change `pick` to `squash` (or `s`) for the commits you want to combine, keeping `pick` for the first commit as the base.

## Interactive Rebase Method

- Run `git rebase -i HEAD~3` to open an editor with the last 3 commits listed ([Git Squash Commits – Squashing the Last N Commits into One Commit](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/git-squash-commits/)).
- Replace `pick` with `squash` (or `s`) for the second and third commits, leaving the first as `pick` ([How to Squash Commits in Git?](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/git/how-to-squash-commits-in-git/)).
- Save the file and git will open another editor for you to write a new combined commit message ([Git Squash Commits – Squashing the Last N Commits into One Commit](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/git-squash-commits/)).

## After Squashing

- If the commits are already pushed to a remote repository, use `git push origin <branch-name> --force` to update the remote with your squashed history ([How to Squash Commits in Git?](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/git/how-to-squash-commits-in-git/)).
- Verify the result by running `git log --oneline` to see the combined commit ([Git Squash Commits – Squashing the Last N Commits into One Commit](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/git-squash-commits/)).

Sources:
1. [Git Squash Commits – Squashing the Last N Commits into One Commit](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/git-squash-commits/)
2. [How to Squash Commits in Git?](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/git/how-to-squash-commits-in-git/)

To set a default value for a column in PostgreSQL using ALTER TABLE, use the `ALTER COLUMN SET DEFAULT` syntax with the column name and the default value you want to assign.

## Basic Syntax

- The standard syntax is `ALTER TABLE table_name ALTER COLUMN column_name SET DEFAULT value;` ([Tutorialsteacher](https://www.tutorialsteacher.com/postgresql/alter-column-default)).

## Examples

- Setting a simple default value: `ALTER TABLE employee ALTER COLUMN salary SET DEFAULT 0;` ([Tutorialsteacher](https://www.tutorialsteacher.com/postgresql/alter-column-default)).
- Setting a function-based default: `ALTER TABLE user_accounts ALTER COLUMN created_at SET DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;` ([Sling Academy](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/postgresql-how-to-set-default-value-for-a-column/)).

## Important Notes

- The new default value only applies to subsequent INSERT or UPDATE commands; existing rows are not affected ([PostgreSQL Documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html)).
- To remove an existing default value, use `ALTER TABLE table_name ALTER COLUMN column_name DROP DEFAULT;` ([Tutorialsteacher](https://www.tutorialsteacher.com/postgresql/alter-column-default)).

To pin a GitHub Action to a commit SHA in your workflow, replace the version tag with the full commit SHA in the `uses` statement. For example, instead of `uses: actions/checkout@v4`, use `uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683`, with an optional comment to keep the version human-readable. This immutable reference guarantees that your workflow runs exactly the code you expect, every time.

## How to Pin an Action

- Replace the version tag with the full commit SHA in your workflow YAML file. Change from `uses: <owner>/<repo>@<version>` to `uses: <owner>/<repo>@<commit-SHA>` ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs: A Practical Security Step](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).
- Find the commit SHA by navigating to the action's repository releases, identifying the release version you want, and copying the corresponding commit hash ([Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security: Everything You Should Know](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide)).
- Add a version comment after the SHA for human readability, though this has no effect on execution ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs: A Practical Security Step](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).

## Why Pinning to SHA Matters

- Commit SHAs are immutable—once a commit exists, its SHA cannot change without changing its content, preventing supply chain attacks where malicious actors could update version tags to point to compromised code ([Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security: Everything You Should Know](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide)).
- GitHub now supports an organization-level policy that can mandate SHA pinning for all actions, including sub-actions that internal action consumers do not control ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs: A Practical Security Step](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).

## Automating Updates

- Use Dependabot to automatically detect SHA-pinned actions and propose updates when new versions are released by adding a configuration to `.github/dependabot.yml` ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs: A Practical Security Step](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).

Sources:
1. [Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs: A Practical Security Step](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)
2. [Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security: Everything You Should Know](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly explains and demonstrates full-SHA pinning without contradicting any reference nugget, though it omits the no-fork requirement, exclusivity of SHA immutability, lack of automatic updates, and repository-level policies.

To roll back a Kubernetes Deployment to a previous revision, use the `kubectl rollout undo` command, which reverts to a prior pod template and performs a rolling update to restore the previous version [kubectl rollout undo - Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_rollout/kubectl_rollout_undo/).

## Basic Rollback Commands

- Roll back to the immediately previous revision with `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name>` [kubectl rollout undo - Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_rollout/kubectl_rollout_undo/)
- Roll back to a specific revision using `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name> --to-revision=<revision-number>` [How to Roll Back a Deployment in Kubernetes Using kubectl](https://k8studio.io/knowledge-base/kubernetes-rollback-deployments/)

## Viewing Revision History

- Check the deployment's revision history with `kubectl rollout history deployment/<deployment-name>` to see all available revisions and their change causes [How to Roll Back a Deployment in Kubernetes Using kubectl](https://k8studio.io/knowledge-base/kubernetes-rollback-deployments/)
- Inspect a specific revision using `kubectl rollout history deployment/<deployment-name> --revision=<number>` [How to \`kubectl rollout undo deployment\` Safely](https://www.plural.sh/blog/kubectl-rollout-undo-deployment/)

## Monitoring and Validation

- Monitor rollback progress with `kubectl rollout status deployment/<deployment-name>` to confirm the rolling update completes successfully [How to Roll Back a Deployment in Kubernetes Using kubectl](https://k8studio.io/knowledge-base/kubernetes-rollback-deployments/)
- Use `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name> --dry-run=server -o yaml` to preview the rollback without making changes [kubectl rollout undo - Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_rollout/kubectl_rollout_undo/)

## Important Limitations

- Rollbacks depend on retained revision history, controlled by `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit` (default: 10), and older revisions may be garbage-collected [How to \`kubectl rollout undo deployment\` Safely](https://www.plural.sh/blog/kubectl-rollout-undo-deployment/)

To build only one stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile, use the `docker build --target <stage>` flag to specify which stage you want to build and stop at [Docker Docs - Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/). By default, Docker builds only the last stage, but `--target` lets you build any named stage instead.

## Using the --target flag

- Name your stages with `AS <name>` in the `FROM` instruction, then reference them with `--target`. For example: `docker build --target build -t myapp:build .` stops the build at the `build` stage ([Docker Multi-Stage Builds](https://dockerbuild.com/tutorials/multi-stage-builds)).
- Without `--target`, `docker build` produces the last stage by default. With BuildKit (the default since Docker 23.0), only the stages that your target depends on are built; unused stages are skipped ([Docker Docs - Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)).

## Common use cases

- Debug a specific stage by building it independently with `--target debug` to inspect intermediate build artifacts ([Docker Docs - Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)).
- Build different variants from one Dockerfile: `docker build --target dev -t myapp:dev .` for development and `docker build --target prod -t myapp:prod .` for production ([Docker Multi-Stage Builds](https://dockerbuild.com/tutorials/multi-stage-builds)).
- Export build artifacts without creating an image using `--target export -o build/out .`, which writes a stage's filesystem to your host ([Docker Multi-Stage Builds](https://dockerbuild.com/tutorials/multi-stage-builds)).

Sources:
1. [Docker Docs - Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/) (partial: a number or identifier in the claim is not on the cited page)

Node.js offers multiple ways to automatically restart your script when files change. The simplest approach is to use Node.js's built-in `--watch` flag (available since v18.11.0), but popular third-party tools like Nodemon and PM2 provide more features and configuration options.

## Built-in Node.js Watch Mode

- Node.js has native watch mode built into the runtime. [To start your application in watch mode, prepend the `--watch` flag](https://salivity.github.io/node.js/article/node-js-watch-mode-how-to-auto-restart-with-watch) to your execution command.

## Using Nodemon (Popular Third-Party Tool)

- [Nodemon is a lightweight, open-source tool designed specifically to monitor Node.js applications for file changes and automatically restart the server](https://www.xjavascript.com/blog/how-to-reload-the-nodejs-app-after-making-changes-to-the-file/). Install it with `npm install --save-dev nodemon` and then run `npx nodemon app.js` or add `"dev": "nodemon app.js"` to your `package.json` scripts. [Nodemon works out of the box, but you can customize its behavior using a `nodemon.json` configuration file](https://www.xjavascript.com/blog/how-to-reload-the-nodejs-app-after-making-changes-to-the-file/) to ignore specific files, watch specific directories, or adjust restart delays.

## Using PM2 (Production-Ready Process Manager)

- [PM2 is a production-grade process manager for Node.js applications that includes a built-in watch mode for auto-reloading](https://www.xjavascript.com/blog/how-to-reload-the-nodejs-app-after-making-changes-to-the-file/). Install globally with `npm install -g pm2`, then start your app with `pm2 start app.js --watch`. [PM2 is designed for both development (auto-reload) and production (monitoring, clustering, logging)](https://www.xjavascript.com/blog/how-to-reload-the-nodejs-app-after-making-changes-to-the-file/).

## Choosing the Right Approach

- [Use Nodemon if you need a lightweight, simple tool focused solely on auto-reloading during development](https://www.xjavascript.com/blog/how-to-reload-the-nodejs-app-after-making-changes-to-the-file/).
- Use Node.js's native `--watch` if you want zero dependencies and are on Node.js v18.11.0 or later.
- [Use PM2 if you want a process manager that handles both development (auto-reload) and production (monitoring, clustering, logging)](https://www.xjavascript.com/blog/how-to-reload-the-nodejs-app-after-making-changes-to-the-file/).

Sources:
1. [To start your application in watch mode, prepend the `--watch` flag](https://salivity.github.io/node.js/article/node-js-watch-mode-how-to-auto-restart-with-watch) (unsupported: the cited page does not contain the quoted text)
2. [Nodemon is a lightweight, open-source tool designed specifically to monitor Node.js applications for file changes and automatically restart the server](https://www.xjavascript.com/blog/how-to-reload-the-nodejs-app-after-making-changes-to-the-file/)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly recommends Node.js’s built-in --watch flag for automatic restarts and does not contradict the reference facts, but it omits the detailed default behavior, path semantics, stability versions, incompatibilities, and missing-file exit status.

To create and activate a Python virtual environment with venv, use `python -m venv` to create it and then run the appropriate activation script for your operating system. A virtual environment is an isolated Python installation that lets you manage project-specific dependencies without affecting other projects or your system Python.

## Creating a virtual environment

- Run `python -m venv .venv` on Unix/macOS or `py -m venv .venv` on Windows to create a new environment in a `.venv` directory ([Install packages in a virtual environment using pip and venv](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/)).
- The venv module creates a directory containing a copy of the Python interpreter, supporting files, and an isolated `site-packages` directory ([`venv` — Creation of virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html)).
- You can specify any directory path as the environment location, not just `.venv` ([12. Virtual Environments and Packages — Python 3.14.8](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/venv.html)).

## Activating a virtual environment

- On Unix/macOS with bash/zsh, run `source .venv/bin/activate` ([Install packages in a virtual environment using pip and venv](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/)).
- On Windows, run `.venv\Scripts\activate` in cmd.exe or `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` in PowerShell ([`venv` — Creation of virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html)).
- After activation, your shell prompt will show the environment name, and `python` will reference that environment's interpreter ([12. Virtual Environments and Packages — Python 3.14.8](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/venv.html)).
- To deactivate, simply type `deactivate` in the terminal ([Install packages in a virtual environment using pip and venv](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/)).

Sources:
1. [Install packages in a virtual environment using pip and venv](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/)
2. [`venv` — Creation of virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html)
3. [12. Virtual Environments and Packages — Python 3.14.8](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/venv.html)

Rust usa um sistema de ownership que gerencia automaticamente a memória sem garbage collector. Cada valor tem exatamente um proprietário, e quando você atribui uma String a outra variável, a propriedade é transferida (chamada de "move"), invalidando a variável original para evitar erros de double free e garantir segurança de memória.

## As três regras de ownership

- [Cada valor em Rust tem exatamente um proprietário](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)
- [Há apenas um proprietário por vez](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)
- [Quando o proprietário sai do escopo, o valor é liberado](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)

## Por que String se move e não é copiada

- [String armazena dados na heap, não na stack como inteiros](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html), portanto ao atribuir `s1` a `s2`, Rust copia apenas o ponteiro, comprimento e capacidade (metadados na stack), não os dados reais
- [Se ambas as variáveis tentassem liberar a mesma memória na heap, causaria um "double free" error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)
- [Rust invalida a variável original para prevenir esse erro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)

## Copy vs Move

- [Tipos primitivos como inteiros implementam o trait Copy e permanecem válidos após atribuição](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)
- [Para copiar explicitamente um tipo não-Copy como String, use .clone()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)

Sources:
1. [Cada valor em Rust tem exatamente um proprietário](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)

judge.rationale: A resposta apresenta corretamente as três regras de ownership, explica o move de String e a prevenção de double free, e distingue tipos Copy que permanecem válidos após atribuição.

O tratamento de erros com `Result` em Rust oferece três principais abordagens: `unwrap`, `expect` e o operador `?`. Cada uma serve a um propósito diferente e deve ser usada em contextos específicos.

## unwrap e expect

- `unwrap()` extrai o valor de sucesso de um `Result`. Se o resultado for `Err`, causa um pânico com mensagem padrão ([Recoverable Errors with Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html)).
- `expect()` funciona como `unwrap()`, mas permite fornecer uma mensagem de erro personalizada que facilita a depuração ([Recoverable Errors with Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html)).
- Em código de produção, `expect()` é preferido porque fornece contexto adicional sobre por que a operação deveria sempre ter sucesso ([Recoverable Errors with Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html)).

## O operador ?

- O operador `?` propaga erros para o chamador em vez de fazer pânico. Se o resultado for `Ok`, extrai o valor; se for `Err`, retorna o erro imediatamente ([Recoverable Errors with Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html)).
- O `?` só pode ser usado em funções cujo tipo de retorno é `Result` ou `Option` ([Recoverable Errors with Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html)).
- O operador também aplica conversão de tipos de erro através da trait `From`, permitindo transformar tipos de erro diferentes ([Recoverable Errors with Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html)).

## Quando usar cada abordagem

- Use `expect()` para situações irrecuperáveis onde o programa não pode continuar, como arquivos de configuração obrigatórios ([Rust error handling explained](https://webcrafted.dev/rust-error-handling-explained-when-to-use-match-and-expect/)).
- Use `?` na maioria das funções de aplicação para propagar erros de forma limpa e concisa ([Rust error handling explained](https://webcrafted.dev/rust-error-handling-explained-when-to-use-match-and-expect/)).
- Evite `unwrap()` em código de produção, pois fornece mensagens genéricas sem contexto ([Rust error handling explained](https://webcrafted.dev/rust-error-handling-explained-when-to-use-match-and-expect/)).

Sources:
1. [Recoverable Errors with Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html)
2. [Rust error handling explained](https://webcrafted.dev/rust-error-handling-explained-when-to-use-match-and-expect/)

judge.rationale: A resposta explica corretamente unwrap, expect e a propagação com ?, mas omite a definição explícita de Result e não menciona o erro E0277 ao usar ? em uma função que retorna ().

Um ambiente virtual Python isola as dependências de cada projeto, permitindo que diferentes projetos usem versões diferentes das mesmas bibliotecas sem conflitos. Para criar, ativar e desativar um ambiente virtual, e congelar as dependências, use os comandos do módulo `venv` integrado ao Python 3.3 ou superior.

## Criar um ambiente virtual

- No Linux ou macOS, use `python3 -m venv .venv` se necessário
- No Windows PowerShell, use `python -m venv C:\caminho\para\novo\ambiente\virtual`
- A pasta `.venv` é uma convenção útil: o ponto deixa o diretório oculto em sistemas Unix, e ferramentas como VS Code reconhecem esse nome

## Ativar o ambiente virtual

- **Linux/macOS (bash/zsh)**: `source .venv/bin/activate` — [o script de ativação prependerá o diretório do ambiente ao seu PATH](https://docs.python.org/pt-br/3/library/venv.html)
- **Windows (Prompt de Comando)**: `.venv\Scripts\activate.bat`
- **Windows (PowerShell)**: `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` — se bloqueado, execute `Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser`
- **Fish shell**: `source .venv/bin/activate.fish`

## Desativar o ambiente virtual

- Para sair do ambiente virtual e voltar ao Python do sistema, digite `deactivate` no seu shell. [O mecanismo exato é específico da plataforma](https://docs.python.org/pt-br/3/library/venv.html).

## Congelar as dependências em requirements.txt

- O arquivo gerado contém as versões exatas de todos os pacotes: `flask==3.1.0`, `requests==2.32.0`, etc.
- Para recriar o ambiente em outra máquina com as mesmas dependências: `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`
- [Você pode usar arquivos de requisitos para congelar os requisitos de um ambiente](https://learn.microsoft.com/pt-br/visualstudio/python/managing-required-packages-with-requirements-txt?view=visualstudio).

## Remover o ambiente virtual

- Como o ambiente é apenas uma pasta, basta apagar: `rm -rf .venv` (Linux/macOS) ou `rmdir /s /q .venv` (Windows CMD). Adicione `.venv/` ao seu `.gitignore` — o `requirements.txt` sim deve ser commitado no Git para permitir que outros recriem o ambiente.

Sources:
1. [A documentação oficial do Python recomenda esse comando para criar ambientes virtuais](https://docs.python.org/pt-br/3/library/venv.html)
2. [O comando mais comum para especificar pacotes dependentes é `pip freeze > requirements.txt`](https://learn.microsoft.com/pt-br/visualstudio/python/managing-required-packages-with-requirements-txt?view=visualstudio)

judge.rationale: A resposta explica criação, ativação, desativação e reinstalação, mas omite no corpo da resposta o comando solicitado `python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt`, essencial para congelar as dependências.

Em JavaScript, `var`, `let` e `const` diferem em escopo, hoisting e capacidade de reatribuição. O `var` possui escopo de função/global e é hoisted com inicialização undefined, permitindo reatribuição e redeclaração. O `let` e `const` possuem escopo de bloco, são hoisted sem inicialização (criando a Temporal Dead Zone), e não permitem redeclaração, mas `let` permite reatribuição enquanto `const` não.

## Escopo

- `var` tem escopo de função ou global, o que significa que as variáveis "vazam" de blocos como loops e condicionais ([var, let, and const in JavaScript](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/differences-between-var-let-const-javascript/)).
- `let` e `const` têm escopo de bloco, ficando confinados às chaves mais próximas, como em loops, funções ou blocos condicionais ([var, let, and const in JavaScript](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/differences-between-var-let-const-javascript/)).

## Hoisting

- `var` é hoisted com um valor padrão de `undefined`, permitindo acesso antes da linha de declaração sem erros ([var, let, and const in JavaScript](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/differences-between-var-let-const-javascript/)).
- `let` e `const` são hoisted, mas permanecem não inicializados durante a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ), resultando em `ReferenceError` ao tentar acessá-los antes da declaração ([JavaScript var let and const](https://www.w3schools.com/Js/js_varletconst.asp)).

## Reatribuição e Redeclaração

- `var` permite tanto reatribuição quanto redeclaração na mesma escopo, o que pode causar bugs ([Difference between var, let and const keywords in JavaScript](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/difference-between-var-let-and-const-keywords-in-javascript/)).
- `let` permite reatribuição mas não redeclaração; tentar redeclarar resulta em erro de sintaxe ([Difference between var, let and const keywords in JavaScript](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/difference-between-var-let-and-const-keywords-in-javascript/)).
- `const` não permite reatribuição nem redeclaração; a variável é imutável após inicialização, embora propriedades de objetos e arrays ainda possam ser modificadas ([JavaScript var let and const](https://www.w3schools.com/Js/js_varletconst.asp)).

Sources:
1. [var, let, and const in JavaScript](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/differences-between-var-let-const-javascript/)
2. [JavaScript var let and const](https://www.w3schools.com/Js/js_varletconst.asp)
3. [Difference between var, let and const keywords in JavaScript](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/difference-between-var-let-and-const-keywords-in-javascript/)

judge.rationale: A resposta explica corretamente escopo, hoisting, reatribuição e mutabilidade da ligação, mas não afirma que declarar const sem inicializador causa SyntaxError.

Git rebase es un comando que reescribe el historial de commits moviendo o reaplicando una serie de confirmaciones sobre una nueva base, creando nuevos commits con nuevos hashes en lugar de simplemente fusionar ramas. El proceso general hace que parezca que tu rama siempre fue creada sobre la base más reciente, resultando en un historial lineal y limpio sin commits de merge innecesarios.

## Cómo funciona git rebase

- El rebase toma los commits de tu rama actual y los reaplica sobre la base especificada, creando nuevas confirmaciones en lugar de mover las originales ([Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/es/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)).
- Existen dos modos principales: el rebase estándar (`git rebase <base>`), que aplica automáticamente todos los commits, y el rebase interactivo (`git rebase -i <base>`), que permite editar, reordenar, fusionar o eliminar commits uno a uno ([Mundobytes](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)).
- Los comandos del rebase interactivo incluyen: pick (usar el commit), reword (editar mensaje), squash (fusionar con anterior), fixup (fusionar descartando mensaje), edit (pausar para modificar contenido) y drop (eliminar commit) ([Mundobytes](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)).

## Cuándo NO usar git rebase

- Nunca reescribas el historial de ramas públicas o compartidas donde otros desarrolladores basan su trabajo, ya que crea commits duplicados y divergencias complicadas ([Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/es/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)).
- Evita rebase en commits que ya han sido compartidos remotamente con otros colaboradores, porque puede resultar en pérdida silenciosa de trabajo ajeno o duplicación de cambios ([LithiumGit](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)).
- Cuando hay conflictos frecuentes en ramas de larga duración, los conflictos en rebase pueden ser confusos y aparecer múltiples veces commit por commit, ya que "ours" y "theirs" están invertidos comparado con merge ([LithiumGit](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)).

## Peligros principales del rebase

- Un `git push --force` sin cautela tras un rebase puede sobrescribir el trabajo de compañeros remotamente; usar `git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes` es más seguro ([LithiumGit](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)).
- Los commits rebasados nunca fueron testeados contra su nueva base, lo que puede dejar cambios intermedios rotos; usar `git rebase --exec "npm test"` verifica cada commit ([LithiumGit](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)).
- El rebase interactivo puede eliminar commits silenciosamente si se borran líneas del archivo de instrucciones; activar `git config --global rebase.missingCommitsCheck error` obliga a usar un comando explícito `drop` ([LithiumGit](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)).

## Recuperación de errores

- Si el rebase está en progreso, `git rebase --abort` restaura el estado anterior a iniciar la operación ([Mundobytes](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)).
- Después de completar un rebase erróneo, `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` recupera la rama inmediatamente, o usa `git reflog show <rama>` días después para encontrar el commit anterior ([LithiumGit](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)).

Sources:
1. [Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/es/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)
2. [Mundobytes](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)
3. [LithiumGit](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)

judge.rationale: La respuesta explica correctamente que rebase reaplica commits sobre una nueva base creando commits nuevos y advierte contra reescribir historial compartido, sin contradecir los nuggets, aunque omite el ancestro común, el proceso basado en diffs, la necesidad de reintegración de colaboradores y `--onto`.

Um desenvolvedor que trabalha com dados pessoais precisa considerar quatro pilares principais da LGPD: direitos dos titulares, responsabilidades do encarregado de dados, notificação de incidentes de segurança e regime de multas. A lei coloca a empresa sob obrigação de garantir proteção, transparência e capacidade de resposta.

## Direitos do Titular (Artigo 18)

- Confirmar a existência de tratamento e acessar todos os dados pessoais: "[o titular] pode confirmar se a empresa trata seus dados e acessar esses dados" ([Direitos dos titulares na LGPD](https://guardiasec.com.br/guia/direitos-dos-titulares-lgpd/))
- Corrigir dados incompletos, inexatos ou desatualizados e exigir que correções sejam propagadas a todos os sistemas e operadores ([Lei 13.709/2018, Art. 18](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2015-2018/2018/lei/l13709compilado.htm))
- Solicitar anonimização, bloqueio ou eliminação de dados desnecessários, excessivos ou tratados em violação à lei ([Lei 13.709/2018, Art. 18](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2015-2018/2018/lei/l13709compilado.htm))
- Obter portabilidade dos dados a outro fornecedor em formato estruturado e utilizável ([Lei 13.709/2018, Art. 18](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2015-2018/2018/lei/l13709compilado.htm))
- Revogar consentimento a qualquer momento: "O consentimento pode ser revogado a qualquer momento mediante manifesta expressão do titular, por procedimento gratuito e facilitado" ([Lei 13.709/2018, Art. 8](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2015-2018/2018/lei/l13709compilado.htm))
- Solicitar revisão de decisões automatizadas que afetem interesses: "[o titular] pode pedir que a empresa revise a decisão e explique os critérios usados" ([Direitos dos titulares na LGPD](https://guardiasec.com.br/guia/direitos-dos-titulares-lgpd/))

## Responsabilidades do Encarregado de Dados (Artigo 41)

- Aceitar reclamações e comunicações dos titulares, prestar esclarecimentos e adotar providências ([Lei 13.709/2018, Art. 41](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2015-2018/2018/lei/l13709compilado.htm))
- Receber comunicações da ANPD (autoridade de proteção de dados) e tomar as medidas cabíveis ([Lei 13.709/2018, Art. 41](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2015-2018/2018/lei/l13709compilado.htm))
- Ter identidade e contato divulgados publicamente no site da empresa: "A identidade e as informações de contato do encarregado deverão ser divulgadas publicamente, de forma clara e objetiva, preferencialmente no sítio eletrônico do controlador" ([Lei 13.709/2018, Art. 41](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2015-2018/2018/lei/l13709compilado.htm))
- Orientar funcionários sobre práticas de proteção de dados e manter canal de atendimento monitorado: "Publicar o contato implica manter o canal funcionando. Uma expressão de agendamento no crontab é composta por cinco campos separados por espaços, cada um representando uma unidade de tempo: minuto, hora, dia do mês, mês e dia da semana. Além dos campos numéricos, o crontab suporta atalhos como @reboot, @daily e outros para simplificar agendamentos comuns.

## Os Cinco Campos

- **Minuto (0-59)**: Define em qual minuto da hora a tarefa é executada. Valores como `*/15` significam a cada 15 minutos (0, 15, 30, 45) ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))
- **Hora (0-23)**: Usa formato de 24 horas onde 0 é meia-noite e 23 é 23h. Horário comercial é representado como `9-17` ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))
- **Dia do Mês (1-31)**: Especifica qual dia do mês executar. O cron lida graciosamente com meses que não possuem 31 dias — a tarefa não será executada se o dia não existir ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))
- **Mês (1-12)**: Os meses podem ser especificados numericamente (1 para janeiro até 12 para dezembro) ou com abreviações de três letras (JAN, FEV, MAR) ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))
- **Dia da Semana (0-7)**: Varia de 0 (domingo) a 6 (sábado), com 7 também válido como domingo. Padrões comuns incluem `1-5` para dias úteis (segunda a sexta-feira) ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))

## Caracteres Especiais

- **Asterisco (*)**: Significa "todos os valores possíveis" para aquele campo. Exemplo: `0 9 * * *` executa todo dia às 9h ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))
- **Vírgula (,)**: Separa múltiplos valores discretos. Exemplo: `0 9,12,15,18 * * *` executa às 9h, meio-dia, 15h e 18h ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))
- **Hífen (-)**: Define intervalos inclusivos. Exemplo: `0 9-17 * * *` executa a cada hora das 9h às 17h ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))
- **Barra (/)**: Especifica incrementos. Exemplo: `*/15 * * * *` executa a cada 15 minutos (0, 15, 30, 45) ([Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html))

## Atalhos Comuns

- **@yearly** ou **@annually**: `0 0 1 1 *` — Uma vez por ano, 1º de janeiro à meia-noite ([Cron Macros: @daily, @hourly, @reboot](https://crontabsheet.com/blog/cron-macros-list.html))
- **@monthly**: `0 0 1 * *` — 1º de cada mês à meia-noite ([Cron Macros: @daily, @hourly, @reboot](https://crontabsheet.com/blog/cron-macros-list.html))
- **@weekly**: `0 0 * * 0` — Todo domingo à meia-noite ([Cron Macros: @daily, @hourly, @reboot](https://crontabsheet.com/blog/cron-macros-list.html))
- **@daily** ou **@midnight**: `0 0 * * *` — Todos os dias à meia-noite ([Cron Macros: @daily, @hourly, @reboot](https://crontabsheet.com/blog/cron-macros-list.html))
- **@hourly**: `0 * * * *` — No início de cada hora ([Cron Macros: @daily, @hourly, @reboot](https://crontabsheet.com/blog/cron-macros-list.html))
- **@reboot**: Executa uma única vez no início do sistema. Disponível apenas em Vixie cron e cronie, não funciona em BSD cron ou implementações modernas em contêineres ([Cron Macros: @daily, @hourly, @reboot](https://crontabsheet.com/blog/cron-macros-list.html))

Sources:
1. [Expressões Cron Explicadas: Guia Completo de Sintaxe](https://run-dev.com/pt/blog/cron-expression-guide.html)
2. [Cron Macros: @daily, @hourly, @reboot](https://crontabsheet.com/blog/cron-macros-list.html)

Pix é um sistema de pagamento instantâneo em tempo real criado e gerenciado pelo [Banco Central do Brasil](https://www.bcb.gov.br/estabilidadefinanceira/pix), oferecido gratuitamente a pessoas físicas e jurídicas, que funciona 24 horas ininterruptamente e foi lançado oficialmente em 16 de novembro de 2020.

## O que é Pix

- Pix é um modo de transferência monetária instantâneo e de pagamento eletrônico em real brasileiro, permitindo transferências entre contas em segundos e disponível para contas corrente, poupança ou pré-pagas ([Banco Central do Brasil](https://www.bcb.gov.br/estabilidadefinanceira/pix)).
- O sistema foi estruturado a partir de 2016 por uma equipe técnica do Banco Central liderada pelo engenheiro Carlos Eduardo Brandt, com os requisitos fundamentais estabelecidos em dezembro de 2018 ([pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pix](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pix)).

## Lançamento e Adoção

- O sistema foi aberto a cadastramento de chaves e testes em 5 de outubro de 2020 e lançado oficialmente de forma integral em 16 de novembro de 2020 ([pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pix](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pix)).
- Alcançou mais de 150 milhões de usuários e se tornou o maior método de pagamento do Brasil, processando 8,6 vezes mais volume de transações que cartões de crédito e débito combinados ([en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pix_(payment_system)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pix_(payment_system))).

Use `Rc<T>` for single-threaded shared ownership of immutable data, and `Arc<T>` when you need thread-safe sharing across multiple threads; the key difference is that `Arc` uses atomic operations for reference counting while `Rc` does not.

## When to use Rc

- `Rc<T>` is appropriate for single-threaded programs where multiple parts of your code need to own the same immutable data, avoiding lifetime parameter complexity ([Rc & Arc - Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/smart-pointers/rc-and-arc/)).
- `Rc` eliminates the need for pervasive lifetime annotations that would otherwise propagate through every struct in your application ([Understanding Rc and Arc in Rust](https://rusteveryday.substack.com/p/understanding-rc-and-arc-in-rust)).
- Common use cases include graph and tree structures where multiple nodes share ownership of a single node, and UI frameworks that share state between components ([Understanding Rc and Arc in Rust](https://rusteveryday.substack.com/p/understanding-rc-and-arc-in-rust)).

## When to use Arc

- `Arc<T>` is required when sharing data across thread boundaries, as `Rc` is not thread-safe and will not compile with threads ([Rc & Arc - Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/smart-pointers/rc-and-arc/)).
- `Arc` is `Send + Sync` if the inner type is, enabling safe data sharing in concurrent code ([Rc & Arc - Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/smart-pointers/rc-and-arc/)).
- For mutable shared state in concurrent contexts, combine `Arc` with a synchronization primitive: `Arc<Mutex<T>>` for exclusive access or `Arc<RwLock<T>>` for multiple readers ([Rc & Arc - Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/smart-pointers/rc-and-arc/)).

## Performance and implementation

- The performance cost of `Arc` versus `Rc` comes solely from atomic operations on reference counts; they use identical memory layout otherwise ([Understanding Rc and Arc in Rust](https://rusteveryday.substack.com/p/understanding-rc-and-arc-in-rust)).
- `Rc::clone()` performs a shallow clone that increments the reference count, not a deep copy of the inner data ([Rc & Arc - Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/smart-pointers/rc-and-arc/)).

## Handling memory cycles

- Both `Rc` and `Arc` can create reference cycles that leak memory; use `Weak<T>` to break cycles, commonly in parent-child relationships where children hold `Weak` references to parents ([Rc & Arc - Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/smart-pointers/rc-and-arc/)).

Sources:
1. [Rc & Arc - Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/smart-pointers/rc-and-arc/)
2. [Understanding Rc and Arc in Rust](https://rusteveryday.substack.com/p/understanding-rc-and-arc-in-rust)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly distinguishes Rc as lower-overhead single-threaded reference counting from Arc as atomic, thread-safe reference counting with conditional Send and Sync, but does not state that Arc stands for Atomically Reference Counted.
