PostgreSQL offers two JSON data types with different storage and performance characteristics: `json` stores data as plain text and preserves formatting, while `jsonb` stores data in a binary format for faster queries and supports indexing.

## Storage and Preservation

- `json` stores an exact copy of the input text, preserving whitespace, key order, and duplicate keys within objects. ([PostgreSQL Documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html))
- `jsonb` parses input into a decomposed binary format at insert time, removing whitespace, sorting keys, and collapsing duplicate keys to their last value. ([PostgreSQL Documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html))

## Performance and Querying

- `jsonb` is significantly faster for queries because it skips reparsing, though insertions are slightly slower due to binary conversion overhead. ([Jam SQL](https://jamsql.com/blog/postgresql-json-jsonb-complete-guide/))
- `json` requires re-parsing on each operation, making it slower for complex queries and searches. ([DbVisualizer](https://www.dbvis.com/thetable/json-vs-jsonb-in-postgresql-a-complete-comparison/))

## Indexing and Advanced Features

- `jsonb` supports GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes for efficient searching across large numbers of documents, plus containment operators and existence tests. ([PostgreSQL Documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html))
- `json` does not support indexing or containment operations. ([DbVisualizer](https://www.dbvis.com/thetable/json-vs-jsonb-in-postgresql-a-complete-comparison/))

## When to Use Each

- Use `jsonb` for nearly all production workloads: dynamic data, complex queries, configuration storage, and when you need indexed nested queries. ([Jam SQL](https://jamsql.com/blog/postgresql-json-jsonb-complete-guide/))
- Use `json` only when you must preserve exact text formatting, perform many insertions without complex queries, or store logs in valid JSON format. ([DbVisualizer](https://www.dbvis.com/thetable/json-vs-jsonb-in-postgresql-a-complete-comparison/))

Sources:
1. [PostgreSQL Documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html)
2. [Jam SQL](https://jamsql.com/blog/postgresql-json-jsonb-complete-guide/)
3. [DbVisualizer](https://www.dbvis.com/thetable/json-vs-jsonb-in-postgresql-a-complete-comparison/)

judge.rationale: The answer accurately states all nine reference facts and directly explains the storage, performance, indexing, preservation, duplicate-key, and usage differences.

HTTP/3 replaces HTTP/2's TCP transport with QUIC over UDP, eliminating head-of-line blocking and reducing connection setup time, while HTTP/3's header compression algorithm QPACK handles out-of-order stream delivery that HTTP/2's HPACK cannot.

## Transport layer differences

- HTTP/2 uses TCP with a three-way handshake that introduces latency; [HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP and combines the cryptographic and transport handshakes](https://www.logicmonitor.com/deep-dive/http3-vs-http2/introduction), enabling [0-RTT resumption for repeat connections](https://www.logicmonitor.com/deep-dive/http3-vs-http2/introduction).
- HTTP/2's TCP causes head-of-line blocking where a lost packet in one stream blocks all subsequent packets; [HTTP/3 with QUIC treats each stream independently so packet loss affects only that stream](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/computer-networks/what-is-http-3-how-it-is-different-from-http-2/).
- [QUIC includes Forward Error Correction mechanisms that allow receivers to reconstruct missing packets without retransmission](https://www.logicmonitor.com/deep-dive/http3-vs-http2/introduction).
- [HTTP/3 supports connection migration using connection IDs instead of IP addresses, allowing uninterrupted service when devices switch networks](https://www.logicmonitor.com/deep-dive/http3-vs-http2/introduction).

## Header compression: HPACK vs QPACK

- [HTTP/2 uses HPACK which maintains synchronized dynamic tables between encoder and decoder, relying on TCP's guaranteed in-order delivery](https://www.dev-toolbox.tech/tools/http-protocol-comparison/examples/hpack-vs-qpack).
- [QPACK, used by HTTP/3, solves the problem of out-of-order stream delivery with dedicated encoder and decoder streams and a known received count mechanism](https://www.dev-toolbox.tech/tools/http-protocol-comparison/examples/hpack-vs-qpack).
- [HPACK and QPACK achieve similar compression ratios of 85–95% reduction in header size, with QPACK's overhead from separate streams minimal despite its added complexity](https://www.dev-toolbox.tech/tools/http-protocol-comparison/examples/hpack-vs-qpack).

Git merge and rebase both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they do so in fundamentally different ways: merge preserves the complete history by creating a new commit with two parents, while rebase rewrites history by replaying your commits as new copies on top of the target branch. You should avoid rebase on shared or public branches because it creates new commit hashes, which causes duplicate commits and diverged history when teammates pull or push.

## How they integrate branches

- **Merge** creates a new "merge commit" with two parents—one pointing to each branch tip—that permanently records when the branches joined. [The existing branches are not changed in any way](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing).
- **Rebase** replays your branch's commits one at a time as brand-new commits on top of the target, creating a linear history with no merge commit. [Git creates F1′ and F2′ as new commits with new hashes; the original F1 and F2 still exist locally but no branch points at them anymore](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git).

## When to avoid rebase: the golden rule

- **Never rebase shared or pushed commits.** [Once you have pushed a branch and a teammate has pulled it, those commits are public. Rebasing them mints new commits with new hashes, so your local history and their local history disagree about what the commits even are](https://generalistprogrammer.com/tutorials/git-rebase-vs-merge).
- **Rebasing a shared branch creates duplicates.** If a teammate still has the original commits and pulls your rebased branch, Git treats the originals and copies as two separate commits and merges them both in, duplicating every change in the history [with no way to tell them apart](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git).
- **Force pushing a rebased branch can erase teammates' work.** After rebase, a normal push is rejected, so developers use `git push --force` to overwrite the remote. [If a teammate pushed commits while you were rebasing, force push throws them away without warning](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git).

## Safe uses of rebase

- **Interactive rebase on unpushed commits** to clean up your history before anyone sees it: squash throwaway "wip" commits, reorder them, or drop debug code. [This is rebase at its best because every example is still local and unpushed, breaking no rules](https://generalistprogrammer.com/tutorials/git-rebase-vs-merge).
- **Use the recommended workflow:** rebase your private feature branch to keep it clean while you work, then merge it into main through a pull request. [This combines the readable feature history from rebase with an honest record of when it merged](https://generalistprogrammer.com/tutorials/git-rebase-vs-merge).
- **If you must push a rebased branch, use `--force-with-lease`** instead of `--force`. [It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it moved since your last fetch, giving you a chance to check what happened](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git).

Sources:
1. [The existing branches are not changed in any way](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing)
2. [Git creates F1′ and F2′ as new commits with new hashes; the original F1 and F2 still exist locally but no branch points at them anymore](https://lithiumgit.com/blogs/the-danger-of-rebase-in-git)
3. [Once you have pushed a branch and a teammate has pulled it, those commits are public. Rebasing them mints new commits with new hashes, so your local history and their local history disagree about what the commits even are](https://generalistprogrammer.com/tutorials/git-rebase-vs-merge)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly explains merge commits, rebasing, linear history, commit replacement, and the shared-history warning, but incorrectly presents merge as always creating a merge commit and omits both three-way merge mechanics and fast-forward merges.

Python lists and tuples are both ordered collections, but lists are mutable (modifiable after creation) while tuples are immutable (fixed after creation). This fundamental difference determines their appropriate use cases and performance characteristics.

## Mutability Differences

- Lists support modification through methods like `append()`, `extend()`, `remove()`, and item assignment, allowing elements to be added, removed, or changed after creation ([Difference Between List and Tuple in Python](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-difference-between-list-and-tuple/)).
- Tuples cannot be modified after creation; attempting to change an element raises a `TypeError` ([Difference Between List and Tuple in Python](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-difference-between-list-and-tuple/)).
- Tuple immutability is shallow—while the tuple itself cannot change, mutable objects stored inside it (like lists) can still be modified ([Python Tuples vs Lists: Differences, Immutability & When to Use Each](https://pythonguruji.com/blog/python-tuples-vs-lists-differences-immutability)).

## Performance and Memory

- Tuples consume less memory and iterate slightly faster than lists because they are immutable and stored in a contiguous memory block ([Difference Between List and Tuple in Python](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-difference-between-list-and-tuple/)).
- Lists require extra space for dynamic resizing to accommodate future modifications, making them less efficient for static data ([Python Tuples vs Lists: Differences, Immutability & When to Use Each](https://pythonguruji.com/blog/python-tuples-vs-lists-differences-immutability)).

## Typical Use Cases

- Use tuples for fixed data that should not change: geographic coordinates, RGB color values, dates, configuration settings, and function return values ([Python Tuples vs Lists: Differences, Immutability & When to Use Each](https://pythonguruji.com/blog/python-tuples-vs-lists-differences-immutability)).
- Use lists when data needs to grow, shrink, or be updated frequently, such as maintaining a dynamic collection of items ([Python Tuples vs Lists: Differences, Immutability & When to Use Each](https://pythonguruji.com/blog/python-tuples-vs-lists-differences-immutability)).
- Tuples can be used as dictionary keys and set elements because they are hashable (when all elements are hashable), whereas lists cannot ([Python Tuples vs Lists: Differences, Immutability & When to Use Each](https://pythonguruji.com/blog/python-tuples-vs-lists-differences-immutability)).

HashMap and BTreeMap are both ordered/unordered map collections in Rust with different trade-offs: HashMap uses hashing for O(1) average lookups but offers no ordering guarantees, while BTreeMap maintains keys in sorted order with O(log n) lookups but provides deterministic iteration and range queries.

## Ordering behavior

- [HashMap is unordered](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-use-btreemap-vs-hashmap/): "Iterating over a HashMap gives you keys in a random sequence that can change between runs."
- [BTreeMap maintains sorted key order](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.BTreeMap.html): "An ordered map based on a B-Tree" with "keys must be of a type that implements the Ord trait, such that two keys can always be compared to determine their Ordering."
- [BTreeMap iteration is deterministic](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-use-btreemap-vs-hashmap/): "Iterating gives you keys from smallest to largest. You get deterministic output and range queries for free."

## Key requirements

- [HashMap requires Hash and Eq](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-use-btreemap-vs-hashmap/): "HashMap requires Hash and Eq. If you have Eq but no Hash, you get a similar bound error."
- [BTreeMap requires Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.BTreeMap.html): Keys must implement the Ord trait for total ordering comparison.
- [BTreeMap works for types without Hash](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-use-btreemap-vs-hashmap/): "Use BTreeMap when your keys don't implement Hash but do implement Ord."

## When to choose each

- [Use HashMap for performance-critical lookups](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/choosing-hashmap-vs-btreemap-trade-offs-in-performance-and-ordering/): "Use HashMap when you need the fastest average-case lookups and insertions" and "when the ordering of elements does not matter."
- [Use BTreeMap for ordered access and range queries](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-use-btreemap-vs-hashmap/): "Use BTreeMap when you need keys sorted or deterministic iteration order" and "when you need range queries, like finding all keys between A and Z."
- [BTreeMap enables efficient range operations](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-use-btreemap-vs-hashmap/): "Range queries are O(log n + k). You pay the log n cost to find the start, then linear cost for the results. HashMap would be O(n) for the same operation."

2. [BTreeMap maintains sorted key order](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.BTreeMap.html)
3. [Use HashMap for performance-critical lookups](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/choosing-hashmap-vs-btreemap-trade-offs-in-performance-and-ordering/)

Rust's `Mutex` and `RwLock` are synchronization primitives that differ in their locking model and when poisoning occurs. `Mutex` provides exclusive access to one thread at a time, while `RwLock` allows multiple concurrent readers or a single exclusive writer ([Mutex in std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html), [RwLock in std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html)).

## Locking differences

- `Mutex` blocks all threads waiting for the lock without distinguishing reader or writer roles; it returns `Result` on lock acquisition. `RwLock` differentiates between read and write locks: `read()` allows concurrent readers as long as no writer holds the lock, while `write()` provides exclusive access and blocks all other readers and writers ([RwLock in std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html)).
- The `read()` and `try_read()` methods on `RwLock` enable parallel access for read-only operations, improving performance in read-heavy workloads compared to `Mutex` which serializes all access ([std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/index.html)).

## Poisoning behavior

- Both `Mutex` and `RwLock` implement poisoning: the lock becomes poisoned if a thread holding it panics. Poisoned locks cause `lock()` and `try_lock()` calls to return a `PoisonError` ([Mutex in std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)).
- `RwLock` poisons only on exclusive write access panics; a panic in a reader does not poison the lock ([RwLock in std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html)).
- `PoisonError` provides an `into_inner()` method to access the guard even after poisoning, allowing recovery. Both locks also provide `clear_poison()` to reset poisoning status after handling ([Mutex in std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)).
